explanations.answer: You do not know what a day may bring
explanations.explanation: That's the reason right in the verse, friend. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, says, "Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring." I've announced a perfect batch before the dough was even mixed, and the oven made a liar out of me. Tomorrow is a batch nobody has peeked at yet.

explanations.answer: Your neighbor will hold it against you
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't mention a neighbor at all, friend. The reason it gives is plain: "…you do not know what a day may bring." Nobody has seen tomorrow's schedule, so there's nothing solid to boast about. Your neighbor can relax, because this one is about what none of us knows.

explanations.answer: Your words will fall back on your head
explanations.explanation: That's a fair-sounding guess, but the verse doesn't say it. It gives one reason: "…you do not know what a day may bring." The problem isn't where the words land, it's that tomorrow isn't ours to promise. I've learned to say "we'll see" before I say "it's guaranteed."

Careful, friend, it's the other way around. The verse says, "Let another praise you, and not your own mouth…" So your own mouth isn't where the praise should come from. I've tried handing myself a trophy, and the applause was very quiet.

Right, it's false. The text says, "Let another praise you, and not your own mouth…" and then adds that a stranger can do it too. Praise lands better when somebody else hands it over. Clapping for yourself in an empty bakery just sounds like a single oven mitt flapping.

Yes, a fool. The verse says a stone is heavy and sand is a burden, but "aggravation from a fool outweighs them both." That's some serious weight. I've hauled a full cookie sheet across a bakery with one mustache, and even that felt lighter.

The verse doesn't say king, friend. It says "aggravation from a fool outweighs them both," meaning the stone and the sand. Nothing here is aimed at rulers. The weight comes from the fool's aggravation, and the verse puts it above the heaviest things on the list.

Close to the kind of word you'd expect, but the verse doesn't use servant. It says the aggravation from a fool is what outweighs a stone and sand. The writer is comparing weights, and the fool's aggravation wins. A stone alone would already sink my cookie box.

That's the one, friend. Solomon says wrath is cruel and anger is like a flood, "but who can withstand jealousy?" He puts jealousy above the other two. That question hangs in the air, and I think nobody in the bakery wants to answer it.

Grief isn't on this list, friend. After wrath and anger, the verse asks, "…but who can withstand jealousy?" The three feelings it lines up are wrath, anger and jealousy. Grief is a real thing, but this verse doesn't name it.

Pride is a good guess, but the verse doesn't use it. Wrath is cruel and anger is like a flood, then comes the question "…who can withstand jealousy?" Jealousy is the one that gets the big question mark. Pride will have to wait for another verse.

Deceitful is right. The verse says, "The wounds of a friend are faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful." A friend might sting you with the truth, but you can trust it. If my friend tells me my hat is crooked, I'd rather hear it before the customers do.

Gentle sounds nice, but the verse says the opposite. It reads, "The wounds of a friend are faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful." The kisses look kind, yet the verse calls them deceitful. Sweet on the outside isn't the same as true.

Rare isn't the word, friend. The verse says the kisses of an enemy are "deceitful." It's talking about whether you can trust them, not how often they come. A wound from a friend is faithful, and a kiss from an enemy is not.

Yes, the full soul. The verse says, "The soul that is full loathes honey…" When you're stuffed, even something sweet turns you off. I've seen a baker push away a cookie after the fortieth sample, and I respected it.

The verse doesn't say proud, friend. It says "The soul that is full loathes honey…" The point is about being full, not about being proud. The same honey looks very different depending on how full you are.
Weary is a fair guess, but that's not the one. The verse says "The soul that is full loathes honey…" Being full is what makes the honey unwelcome. A weary soul isn't mentioned here at all.
True. The verse says, "…but to a hungry soul, any bitter thing is sweet." When you're hungry enough, even bitter things taste good. Hunger changes what counts as a treat, friend.

It's actually true, friend. The verse says, "…but to a hungry soul, any bitter thing is sweet." It sets that against the full soul that loathes honey. Same world, different appetites, and that's the whole picture.

explanations.answer: A bird that strays from its nest
explanations.explanation: That's the picture. The verse says, "Like a bird that strays from its nest is a man who wanders from his home." A nest is where a bird belongs, and the verse puts a man's home in that same place. I know a little about being far from a warm spot, and I'd rather be near mine.

explanations.answer: A sheep that strays from its flock
explanations.explanation: Sheep and flocks show up later in this chapter, but not here. This verse says, "Like a bird that strays from its nest is a man who wanders from his home." The picture is a bird and its nest. Home is the part that matters.

explanations.answer: A ship that drifts from its harbor
explanations.explanation: A ship is a nice picture, but it isn't in the verse. The text says, "Like a bird that strays from its nest is a man who wanders from his home." So the comparison is a bird and a nest. No harbor, no sails, just a little bird far from where it belongs.

Friend is it. The verse says, "Oil and incense bring joy to the heart, and the counsel of a friend is sweetness to the soul." Good advice from a friend is as welcome as a warm oven on a cold morning. Hearing it from somebody who cares makes it go down easy.

Teacher is a fine job, but the verse doesn't use it. It says "the counsel of a friend is sweetness to the soul." The sweetness comes from a friend. I teach for a living, and even I think the verse is right.

The verse doesn't say prophet, friend. It says, "…the counsel of a friend is sweetness to the soul." It's the advice of a friend that brings that sweetness. Oil and incense bring joy to the heart, and a friend's counsel joins them on the list.
True. The verse says, "…better a neighbor nearby than a brother far away." Someone close enough to help beats a relative who's too far to reach. I'd take the one who can knock on my door.

It's actually true, friend. The verse says, "…better a neighbor nearby than a brother far away." Being close counts for a lot when trouble shows up. The neighbor is the one who can actually get there.

explanations.answer: Answer the one who taunts him
explanations.explanation: Right. The speaker says, "Be wise, my son, and bring joy to my heart, so that I can answer him who taunts me." A wise son gives him something to say back. I think there's a proud dad in there somewhere.

explanations.answer: Rest easy in his old age
explanations.explanation: Resting easy sounds lovely, but the verse doesn't say it. It says "…so that I can answer him who taunts me." Nothing about old age appears there. The wise son gives his father an answer for the one who taunts him.

explanations.answer: Pass on his land in peace
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't mention land, friend. The speaker says, "Be wise, my son, and bring joy to my heart, so that I can answer him who taunts me." So the result is being able to answer the one who taunts. A wise son gives his father something to say back.

Flip that one, friend. The verse says, "The prudent see danger and take cover, but the simple keep going and pay the penalty." The prudent are the ones who take cover. The simple walk right on through it.

False is right. The verse says, "The prudent see danger and take cover, but the simple keep going and pay the penalty." Same danger, but the prudent step aside and the simple don't. I've seen smoke from an oven and gone to open a window, and I recommend it.
His garment is right. The verse says, "Take the garment of him who posts security for a stranger…" That's the advice Solomon gives. It's like holding the apron until the job is done.
A sandal is close in spirit, but the verse says garment. It reads, "Take the garment of him who posts security for a stranger…" Clothing is what gets taken. A sandal is not on the list.

A signet ring sounds official, but the verse doesn't name one. It says, "Take the garment of him who posts security for a stranger…" A garment is what the text names. My own handle has a name carved on it, but that's a different story.

Curse is the word. The verse says, "If one blesses his neighbor with a loud voice early in the morning, it will be counted to him as a curse." Early and loud turns a blessing sour. Some blessings come better at a reasonable hour with the volume down.

Kindness would be the hope, but the verse says otherwise. It reads, "…it will be counted to him as a curse." A loud voice early in the morning changes how the blessing is received. The words may be kind and still land the wrong way.

A gift is a nice thought, but that's not what the verse says. It says the loud morning blessing "will be counted to him as a curse." The neighbor hears something very different from what was meant. Timing and volume count.

Yes, the wind. The verse says restraining her is "like holding back the wind or grasping oil with one's right hand." Both are things you can't really get a grip on. I've tried to catch wind in my apron, and all I got was a flappy apron.

The verse doesn't mention building, friend. It says restraining her is "like holding back the wind or grasping oil with one's right hand." So the other picture is the wind. Sand shows up earlier in the chapter, but only as a burden.

A donkey isn't in the verse. It says restraining her is "like holding back the wind or grasping oil with one's right hand." The second picture is the wind. Two things that slip right through your hands.

Sharpens is the word. The verse says, "As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another." Two tough things rubbing together leave each one sharper. I spent years soft around the edges, so I know who I'd like next to me.
Testing shows up in verse 21 of this chapter, but not here. This verse says, "As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another." Iron against iron makes each one sharper. The key word is sharpens.

Wearing down is the opposite of what the verse says. It reads, "As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another." The rubbing makes an edge, not a stub. I've been worn down before, and sharp is much better.

Master fits the first blank. The verse says, "Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and he who looks after his master will be honored." The fig tree and the master go together: care for one, and you eat the fruit. Look after the other, and you're honored.

Honored fits the second blank. The verse says the one who looks after his master "will be honored." Just like tending the tree gets you the fruit, looking after someone gets you honor. Care leads to reward in both halves.

Brother is not what the verse says. It says "he who looks after his master will be honored." Brothers do come up earlier in this chapter, in verse 10, but not in this line. The person being looked after here is the master.

Forgotten is the opposite of the verse. It says the one who looks after his master "will be honored." Being honored is the result of that care. I've been forgotten before, so I'm glad that's not how this one ends.
Rich is a tempting word, but the verse doesn't use it. It says the one who looks after his master "will be honored." The reward is honor, not riches. Honor is a different kind of payday.
The heart is right. The verse says, "As water reflects the face, so the heart reflects the true man." Look into still water and you see your face. Look at the heart and you see the true man.

The tongue is a good guess, but the verse doesn't say it. It says, "As water reflects the face, so the heart reflects the true man." The heart is the mirror here. A tongue can say a lot of things, but the verse points deeper.

Hands do a lot of work, but the verse says heart. It reads, "As water reflects the face, so the heart reflects the true man." The heart is what shows who a man truly is. My mustache does most of my work, but it's not the answer either.

True. The verse says, "Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied; so the eyes of man are never satisfied." The eyes keep wanting more, just like those two. I've been guilty of eyeing one more cookie, and then another.

It's true, friend. The verse says, "Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied; so the eyes of man are never satisfied." It puts the eyes of man in the same line as those two. Wanting more never seems to fill up.

Praise is the answer. The verse says, "A crucible for silver and a furnace for gold, but a man is tested by the praise accorded him." Fire tests metal, and praise tests a man. Being cheered can be tougher than it sounds.

Wealth is not what the verse names. It says, "…but a man is tested by the praise accorded him." So the test is praise, not riches. I've never had a pile of gold, but I have had a good compliment, and it did test me.

Battles aren't in this verse. It says, "…but a man is tested by the praise accorded him." Silver and gold get their tests by fire, and a man gets his by praise. It's a quieter kind of test, but the verse says it counts.

explanations.answer: It will not depart from him
explanations.explanation: That's it. The verse says, "Though you grind a fool like grain with mortar and a pestle, yet his folly will not depart from him." Even grinding him like grain doesn't remove it. Some things don't come out no matter how hard you press.

explanations.answer: It is crushed away for good
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what the verse says. It reads, "Though you grind a fool like grain with mortar and a pestle, yet his folly will not depart from him." The grinding doesn't get rid of it. The folly stays put.

The verse has no chaff in it, friend. It says, "Though you grind a fool like grain with mortar and a pestle, yet his folly will not depart from him." Nothing blows away. The folly stays right where it was.

That's the reason given. The verse says, "…for riches are not forever, nor does a crown endure to every generation." What you have now won't last by itself. So you pay attention to it, the way I check the oven timer.

The verse doesn't mention thieves. It says to keep watch "for riches are not forever, nor does a crown endure to every generation." The reason is that riches don't last. Nobody is sneaking around in this verse.

No king is counting anything here, friend. The verse gives the reason: "…for riches are not forever, nor does a crown endure to every generation." Even a crown doesn't last through every generation. The reason is that riches don't last.

Clothing is right. The verse says, "the lambs will provide you with clothing, and the goats with the price of a field." Lambs cover your back, and goats can buy you a field. Looking after the flock has real payoffs.

Silver appeared in verse 21 of this chapter, but not here. This verse says, "the lambs will provide you with clothing, and the goats with the price of a field." Lambs give clothing. The goats are the ones tied to the price of a field.

Shelter makes sense, but it's not the word. The verse says, "the lambs will provide you with clothing, and the goats with the price of a field." The lambs give you clothing. A nice warm coat is a good thing, anyway.

Not quite, friend. The verse says, "You will have plenty of goats' milk to feed you—food for your household and nourishment for your maidservants." So the milk feeds you and your household, and your maidservants too. Nobody gets left out.

False is right. The verse says there will be plenty of goats' milk to feed you, with "food for your household and nourishment for your maidservants." So the milk is for you and the household, not just you. There's enough to go around.
